text: Lesson four covered the cost of poor data in the abstract. Lesson twenty-five turned that into a specific gap list for your organization. Now it's time to turn that gap list into something that actually gets funded.

Nobody gets governance funded by asserting it's important. It gets funded the same way any other initiative does — with a defined problem, a proposed solution, a resource ask, and a way to measure whether it worked.

Four components, every time. The problem in business terms, not technical ones. The proposed solution and scope — usually a scoped pilot, not a company-wide rollout. The resources required, including sponsorship itself. And the anticipated value, tied to something the audience already tracks.

The same program gets framed three different ways, because each stakeholder is weighing a different risk. A CFO weighs cost avoidance and audit exposure. A CIO weighs operational risk and technical debt. A business unit leader weighs speed and trust in the numbers their team already uses every day.

A business case without a real gap list behind it reads generic — every governance pitch says roughly the same thing about trust and quality. The gap list is what makes it specific: the actual weak dimension, the actual pain already visible, named plainly instead of hinted at.

Problem, solution, resources, value — framed for the audience in the room, grounded in your own gap list. That's a business case someone can actually say yes to. Next up: what you actually do once they say yes — starting small, with a governance pilot.
